title: Much of the fight is logomachy over calling assurance divine-faith certainty
source_text: XLIII. Unde jure merito videri potest hic multum esse logomachiae, & verbalis contentionis; quandoquidem non eodem sensu negant & affirmant Doctores utriusque communionis certitudinem fidei divinae inesse illi persuasioni, quam qui fide per charitatem operante praediti sunt habere possunt & debent de sua coram Deo justificatione. Cum enim inter utrosque conveniat unde nascatur, & quibus fundamentis nitatur illa certitudo, nempe, altera propositione diserte & clare verbo Dei expressa, altera vero quae nobis innotescit conscientiae nostrae testimonio, & interno quodam sensu, quo fidem & poenitentiam propriam percipimus, Protestantibus talis certitudo videtur dici posse fidei divinae, quia Dei testimonio, etiamsi non solo nititur; Romanensibus vero contrarium videtur, quia non nititur solo Dei testimonio, sed altera propositione, quae non aeque certa est, ac illa quae expresse verbo Dei traduntur: juxta Philosophos autem in Syllogismis conclusio censetur sequi partem debiliorem.
pass_a_gloss: Whence with good right it can seem that here there is much logomachy and verbal contention; since it is not in the same sense that the doctors of each communion deny and affirm that the certainty of divine faith inheres in that persuasion which those endowed with faith working through love can and ought to have concerning their justification before God. For since it is agreed between both whence that certainty arises and on what foundations it rests—namely, on one proposition expressly and clearly set out in God’s Word, and on another which becomes known to us by the testimony of our conscience and by a certain inward sense by which we perceive our own faith and repentance—to Protestants such certainty seems able to be called of divine faith, because it rests on God’s testimony even if not on it alone; but to the Romanists the contrary seems, because it does not rest on God’s testimony alone, but on another proposition which is not equally certain as those things which are expressly handed down by God’s Word: and according to the Philosophers, in syllogisms the conclusion is judged to follow the weaker part.
pass_b_english: Shared foundations, quarreling labels: Protestants still say ‘divine faith’; Rome refuses because of the weaker experiential premise.
Le Blanc flags a classic logomachy under the syllogism’s weaker-part rule.
